## Proof

We determine the cardinality of the set $\mathcal{F}$ of increasing (strictly increasing) functions $f:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$. The same argument applies *mutatis mutandis* to weakly increasing functions, and we note at the end why the answer is identical in that case.

### Upper bound

Every increasing function is in particular a function $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$, so
$$\mathcal{F}\subseteq \mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{Z}}.$$
Since $|\mathbb{Z}|=\aleph_0$, we have $|\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{Z}}|=\aleph_0^{\aleph_0}=2^{\aleph_0}$. Hence $|\mathcal{F}|\le 2^{\aleph_0}$.

### Lower bound

We exhibit an injection $\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}\hookrightarrow \mathcal{F}$, where $\mathbb{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$.

For each subset $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, define $f_A:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ by
$$f_A(n)=\begin{cases} n, & n\le 0,\\[4pt] n+\bigl|A\cap\{1,2,\dots,n\}\bigr|, & n\ge 1.\end{cases}$$

**$f_A$ is strictly increasing.** For $n\le -1$, $f_A(n+1)-f_A(n)=1$. At the transition, $f_A(0)-f_A(-1)=0-(-1)=1$. For $n\ge 1$,
$$f_A(n+1)-f_A(n)=1+\mathbf{1}_{n+1\in A}\ge 1.$$
So $f_A(n+1)>f_A(n)$ for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}$.

**The map $A\mapsto f_A$ is injective.** From $f_A$ we recover $|A\cap\{1,\dots,n\}|=f_A(n)-n$ for $n\ge 1$, and hence recover $A$ via
$$n\in A \iff \bigl(f_A(n)-n\bigr)-\bigl(f_A(n-1)-(n-1)\bigr)=1.$$
Thus distinct subsets $A$ yield distinct functions $f_A$.

Since $|\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{N}}|=2^{\aleph_0}$, we obtain $|\mathcal{F}|\ge 2^{\aleph_0}$.

### Conclusion

Combining the two bounds,
$$|\mathcal{F}|=2^{\aleph_0},$$
the cardinality of the continuum.

### Remark on the weakly increasing interpretation

If "increasing" is read as *non-decreasing* (weakly increasing), the set $\mathcal{F}_{\le}$ of such functions satisfies
$$\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathcal{F}_{\le}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{Z}},$$
where $\mathcal{F}$ is the strictly increasing family. The lower bound $|\mathcal{F}|\ge 2^{\aleph_0}$ and upper bound $|\mathbb{Z}^{\mathbb{Z}}|\le 2^{\aleph_0}$ therefore squeeze $|\mathcal{F}_{\le}|$ to the same value $2^{\aleph_0}$.

In either interpretation, the cardinality of the set of increasing functions $\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ is $\boxed{2^{\aleph_0}}$.
